Start with a controlled physical registration test on the copies. The marks provide a constraint independent of whether anything looks like a word.

1. Label the copies A and B and record each dot's original corner and which face is toward you. Hold A fixed. Compare the positions of the four marks, including their order and spacing.
2. With the rectangular outlines coincident, try B rotated 180 degrees in its plane, then B turned over about a vertical axis. Both can bring B's right edge to A's left, but the rotation reverses the marks' vertical order whereas the turnover preserves it. Record which, if either, matches all four marks. The dots and asymmetric strokes help distinguish these operations; do not assume the dots themselves must coincide. If neither fits, test registration by translation without requiring coincident outlines and record how much of the cards actually overlaps. Do not stretch or independently adjust strokes.
3. For each alignment that satisfies the registration marks, examine the entire combined pattern. Are complementary strokes becoming consistently oriented characters? Is there a clear reading order? A few suggestive fragments are weaker evidence than a coherent result across the cards.

Then test the title more literally. Trace the two cards in different colors so you can distinguish shared strokes from strokes contributed by only one card. Compare three views: the union of all strokes, the shared portions, and the nonshared portions. An ordinary black overlay shows the union; it may conceal which black strokes coincide, so it cannot by itself adequately test the other two views.

These tests can distinguish a rotation from a reflection, establish whether registration is sufficient to constrain the overlay, and test whether “Same difference” refers to common versus differing material. If several orientations satisfy symmetric registration marks, preserve that ambiguity until the strokes supply additional evidence. No alignment has been executed here, and there is not enough visual information to predict the resulting characters.

The symbols strongly suggest the eight I Ching trigrams: three lines, each solid or broken, give exactly eight forms. That identifies a promising vocabulary, but does not establish what the pairs, compass, or arrows do.

The next useful artifact is a literal transcription. Record every symbol as three bits, explicitly using top-to-bottom order and solid = 1; retain pair order, page position, every arrow's endpoints, and any compass labels. Keep this neutral encoding separate from later trigram conventions, which commonly count lines from the bottom. Without the page, I cannot supply that transcription or report patterns in it.

Develop two interpretations in parallel:

• Paired trigrams as hexagrams. Stacking two three-line symbols produces a six-line hexagram. Determine whether the page's layout indicates which member is upper and which lower; otherwise retain both possibilities. Repeated pairs should produce repeated hexagrams, and swapped pairs should exchange their upper and lower halves. All 64 possible combinations are valid hexagrams, so merely obtaining valid hexagrams does not confirm this route. A stronger check is whether arrows consistently represent a particular line change, or whether hexagram identities explain additional printed structure. Without a legend or answer format, converting arbitrary hexagram numbers directly into letters would add an unsupported step.

• Trigrams as compass positions. Trigrams have traditional directional arrangements. For example, the Later Heaven arrangement associates water with north, mountain with northeast, thunder with east, wind with southeast, fire with south, earth with southwest, lake with west, and heaven with northwest. Earlier Heaven uses a different arrangement. Check whether labels or spatial organization distinguish them, including how north is oriented on this page; do not select an arrangement simply because it gives attractive output. A pair might specify two endpoints or successive bearings, but that remains a hypothesis.

Before choosing either route, inspect arrow-linked pairs structurally. If a link from (a,b) to (c,d) repeatedly has b = c, that supports a sequence of transitions without requiring any compass assignment. If linked symbols consistently differ at one particular line, that instead supports a line-change operation. Count changed lines within pairs as well. Either observation would be more discriminating than trying numerous alphabet encodings. If neither occurs, retain the trigram identification while leaving the roles of compass and arrows unresolved.

The five-letter word is a candidate produced by a flexible search. Replacing three labels after trying many orders and shifts substantially weakens its evidential value. It establishes that one chosen labeling and extraction can yield a plausible word; it does not establish the intended labels, mechanism, reading order, or solution. The word could still be correct, but presently lacks independent structural support.

Freeze the original object labels and the exact extraction that produced the candidate. The next investigation should use information the search has neglected: coordinates, abnormal states, and the empty cell. Make a 5-by-5 inventory with each original label, its row and column, its literal visible state, and whether it neighbors the blank. For each unusual object, separate the observation (“cup lying on its side”) from possible interpretations (“left,” “tipped,” “spilled”). A sideways cup alone does not establish a directional instruction.

Use that inventory to discriminate among these possibilities:

• The five unusual objects select five entries. Check whether there is exactly one in each row or column. If so, the grid supplies a natural ordering worth testing once with the frozen labels. Then ask what their states contribute and why the blank occupies its particular position. A direct selection becomes convincing only if those features also have a rule; obtaining another five-letter fragment alone is insufficient.

• The blank enables movement. A grid containing 24 objects and one vacancy invites a sliding or displacement interpretation. Check whether an explicitly directional unusual object is adjacent to the vacancy and uniquely indicates a legal move into it. Track the resulting vacancy and ask whether the same rule determines the next move. Orthogonal adjacency and a reusable instruction are concrete checks. If the first move requires an arbitrary choice or a distant jump, do not launch an unconstrained sliding-puzzle search.

• Rows or columns encode relationships or a missing member. Look for a consistent classification or progression among the ordinary objects, with unusual states breaking or modifying that rule. A useful model should predict what belongs in the empty cell, or why that location must be empty, using the same rule across several rows or columns. The 5-by-5 dimensions alone do not justify importing a Polybius alphabet.

Choose the next branch by its cheapest discriminating check: count abnormal entries by row and column, inspect their actual states, and identify the blank's neighbors. Before extracting another word, write down a prediction about a relationship not used to construct the hypothesis. All labels have already been seen, so this is a consistency test, not fresh unseen evidence. With no image or oracle, I cannot perform these checks. The most useful additional description is the coordinate-and-state inventory, especially the blank and its neighbors, rather than another set of synonyms.
